concepts.name: Dynamics
concepts.statement: Dynamics is the study of the forces that cause objects and systems to move. Kinematics describes how an object moves, and dynamics asks why it moves that way; Newton’s laws of motion are its foundation.

concepts.name: Force
concepts.statement: A force is a push or a pull, and it has both a magnitude and a direction, so it is a vector and adds as other vectors add.

concepts.name: External force
concepts.statement: Only the forces that act on a body from outside it change its motion, so before any law can be applied the forces have to be sorted into those that come from outside and those that act between parts of the body. A body cannot push itself along.

concepts.name: Draw a free-body diagram
concepts.statement: A free-body diagram draws the body as a single point and every external force acting on it as an arrow from that point, so the forces can be added without the picture of the situation getting in the way.

concepts.name: Standard unit of force
concepts.statement: A force can be measured only against some force that can be produced again and again, just as a distance is measured against a standard distance. The stretched spring gives such a standard, and the magnitude of any other force can then be stated as a multiple of it.

concepts.name: Free-body diagram
concepts.statement: A free-body diagram is a sketch showing all of the external forces acting on an object or system, with the system represented by a dot and the forces by arrows extending outward from it.

concepts.name: Newton’s first law of motion
concepts.statement: A body at rest remains at rest, and a body in motion remains in motion at a constant velocity, unless a net external force acts on it. The law says that a change in velocity has a cause, so a sliding object that stops has been stopped by something, and friction is that something.

concepts.name: Inertia
concepts.statement: Inertia is the property of a body that keeps it at rest or keeps it moving at a constant velocity, which is why Newton’s first law is also called the law of inertia. Some bodies have more of it than others, and that difference is what mass measures.

concepts.name: Mass
concepts.statement: Mass is the quantity of matter in a body, and it is how much inertia the body has. Unlike weight, mass does not vary with location: a body has the same mass on Earth, in orbit and on the Moon, and masses are found in practice by comparison with the standard kilogram.

concepts.name: Define the system of interest
concepts.statement: Which forces count as external depends on where the boundary of the system is drawn, so the boundary has to be chosen before Newton’s second law can be written down. The wagon and its rider make one system; the wagon alone makes another, and the two give different net forces.

forms.condition: the professor, the cart and the equipment taken as one system
the cart and the equipment taken as the system

concepts.name: Net external force
concepts.statement: The net external force is the vector sum of all the external forces acting on a system, found head to tail or by components as any other vectors are. It is the single force that stands in for all of them, and it is what the second law relates to the acceleration.

forms.condition: the two applied forces are perpendicular

concepts.name: Newton’s second law of motion, $\kFnet = m\ka$
concepts.statement: The acceleration of a system is directly proportional to the net external force on it and in the same direction, and inversely proportional to its mass. It is a relation among three quantities that can each be measured on their own, not a definition.

forms.condition: only the magnitudes of the force and the acceleration are considered

concepts.name: The newton, $1\ \text{N} = 1\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m/s}^2$
concepts.statement: The SI unit of force is defined from Newton’s second law: one newton is the force that accelerates a one-kilogram system at one meter per second squared.

concepts.name: Weight, $\kwgt = m\kg$
concepts.statement: The weight of an object is the gravitational force on it, and Newton’s second law applied to a falling object gives its magnitude as the mass times the acceleration due to gravity. Weight is a force and is measured in newtons, and it changes with the body the object is near.

concepts.name: Mass against weight
concepts.statement: Mass is the quantity of matter and does not change with place; weight is the gravitational force on that mass and does. The two words are used interchangeably in everyday language, but in physics they mean different things.

concepts.name: Friction
concepts.statement: Friction is a force that opposes the motion past each other of objects that are touching. It is an external force, and it is what slows a sliding object down.

concepts.name: System
concepts.statement: A system is the object or collection of objects being observed, defined by its boundaries. All forces originating from outside the system are external forces.

concepts.name: Newton’s third law of motion
concepts.statement: Whenever one body exerts a force on a second body, the first body experiences a force equal in magnitude and opposite in direction to the force it exerts. Forces always occur in pairs, and no body can exert a force on another without experiencing one itself.

concepts.name: The two forces of a pair act on different bodies
concepts.statement: The two forces of a third-law pair look as though they should cancel, and they do not, because they act on different systems. The wall pushes on the swimmer’s feet and the swimmer’s feet push on the wall, and only the first of those is an external force on the swimmer.

concepts.name: Internal forces cancel and do not enter the second law
concepts.statement: A force between two parts of one system is matched by its equal and opposite partner inside the same system, so the two add to nothing and the net external force is unchanged. That is why the professor’s push on the cart does not appear when the professor and the cart are taken as one system.

concepts.name: Thrust
concepts.statement: Thrust is the forward reaction force on a rocket that throws gas backward: it pushes hard on the gas, and by the third law the gas pushes just as hard forward on the rocket. Thrust drives rockets, airplanes and cars.

concepts.name: Normal force $\kN$
concepts.statement: Whatever supports a load must push up on it, and where that support is perpendicular to the surface of contact it is called the normal force. A table sags under a bag of dog food until its restoring force is as large as the weight, and on a level surface that makes the normal force equal to the weight; on an incline, or when the object accelerates, it is not.

forms.condition: an object at rest on a horizontal surface that is not accelerating

concepts.name: Weight on an incline, $\kwpar = m\kg\sin\theta$ and $\kwperp = m\kg\cos\theta$
concepts.statement: On a slope the convenient axes are along and across the surface, and the weight is the one force that lies along neither, so it is resolved into a component parallel to the slope, which drives the object down it, and a component perpendicular to it, which the normal force balances.

forms.condition: an incline that makes an angle θ with the horizontal
an incline that makes an angle θ with the horizontal
there is no motion perpendicular to the slope

concepts.name: Acceleration down a frictionless incline, $\kapar = \kg\sin\theta$
concepts.statement: Dividing the parallel component of the weight by the mass cancels the mass, so every object slides down a frictionless incline of the same angle with the same acceleration, just as every object falls with the same acceleration in the absence of air resistance.

forms.condition: friction on the incline is negligible

concepts.name: Tension
concepts.statement: A tension is a force carried along the length of a flexible connector such as a rope, a cable or a tendon. A connector can only pull, never push, so the force it carries is always parallel to its length, and where there is no friction the tension is the same everywhere along it.

concepts.name: Tension in a rope supporting a weight, $\kTf = m\kg$
concepts.statement: A mass hanging at rest from a rope has no acceleration, so the net force on it is zero and the tension must equal the weight. Once the tension is known at one point of a frictionless connector it is known everywhere along it.

forms.condition: a rope of negligible mass supporting a stationary object

concepts.name: Tension from a perpendicular force, $\kTf = \kFperp / (2\sin\theta)$
concepts.statement: Pushing sideways at the middle of a connector that is nearly straight creates a tension far larger than the push, because only the small vertical component of each half supports it. That is how a car is pulled out of the mud with a chain, and it is why no connector can be exactly horizontal.

forms.condition: a force perpendicular to the length of a flexible connector, exerted at its middle
a weight at the middle of a connector that sags by an angle θ on either side

concepts.name: Inertial frame of reference
concepts.statement: An inertial frame of reference is a frame that is neither accelerating nor rotating, and only in such a frame do Newton’s laws take their simple forms. In an accelerating frame an observer sees forces with no physical origin, such as the westward push on a satellite seen from a rotating Earth, and those fictitious forces are an artifact of the frame.

concepts.name: The four steps for a problem about forces
concepts.statement: A problem about forces is worked in the same four steps every time: sketch the situation and draw every force as an arrow, list the knowns and unknowns and choose the system of interest, draw the free-body diagram and apply Newton’s second law, and check that the answer and its units are reasonable.

concepts.name: Net force along each axis, $\kFnetx = m\ka$ and $\kFnety = 0$
concepts.statement: Before the force equations are written, decide in which directions the system accelerates. Where there is no acceleration along an axis the net force along that axis is zero, and where there is, the net force along it is the mass times that acceleration; the two axes are then two one-dimensional problems.

forms.condition: the system accelerates along the x-axis
friction of magnitude f opposes the motion down the incline
the system has no acceleration along the y-axis

concepts.name: Resolve forces onto convenient axes
concepts.statement: A two-dimensional force problem becomes a pair of one-dimensional problems as soon as the forces are projected onto a well-chosen pair of axes: one axis along the direction of motion, or along an incline, saves most of the work.

concepts.name: Two wires at different angles carry different tensions
concepts.statement: When an object hangs from two wires the horizontal components of the tensions must cancel and the vertical components must add to the weight. The two tensions are equal only when the two angles are equal; the wire that is nearer the vertical carries the greater share.

forms.condition: an object hanging at rest from two wires

concepts.name: What a scale reads, $\kFs = m\ka + m\kg$
concepts.statement: A bathroom scale reads the force it pushes up with, not the weight. In an elevator accelerating upward it reads more than the weight, at any constant velocity it reads the weight exactly, and in free fall it reads zero and the person appears weightless.

forms.condition: a person standing on a scale in a system accelerating vertically

concepts.name: Drag force
concepts.statement: A drag force is the frictional force a fluid such as air or water exerts on an object moving through it, and like any friction it opposes the motion.

forms.condition: the drag is opposite to the applied force and the motion is along one line

concepts.name: Join kinematics to Newton’s laws in one problem
concepts.statement: Forces produce accelerations, and an acceleration is what the kinematic equations are written in, so a problem can be worked from a force to a distance or from a distance back to a force. Identify which principles are involved, then use each chapter’s own strategy in turn.

concepts.name: The four basic forces
concepts.statement: Only four distinct forces account for every known phenomenon: the gravitational, the electromagnetic, the weak nuclear and the strong nuclear force. Everything we feel directly except gravity is electromagnetic, and the two nuclear forces act only over the size of a nucleus or less.

concepts.name: Force field
concepts.statement: All forces act at a distance, so something must carry them between objects. A force field surrounds the object that creates it and is a characteristic of that object alone; a test object placed in the field experiences a force that depends on where it is.

concepts.name: Carrier particle
concepts.statement: Fields leave open what actually carries a force, and the proposal that has held since Yukawa is that every force is transmitted by the exchange of an elementary particle, as two people passing a basketball push each other apart without touching.
